newsitem.title: JAPAN: France-Japan accord sets sights on space research.
newsitem.headline: France-Japan accord sets sights on space research.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday signed a far-reaching agreement on bilateral relations with stepped up cooperation in space research, including joint satellite development, as its centrepiece.

The treaty, called "20 Points For The Year 2000", includes agreements to hold annual summit meetings, twice-yearly meetings of foreign ministers and other measures to take ties between the two nations to a loftier level.

"We are two great economic powers, the second and the fourth in the world, and yet our exchanges are insufficient -- Japan is represented in only two percent of the French market and France in only 1.7 percent of the Japanese market," Chirac told reporters.
Hashimoto said: "We were able to start on making our bilateral relationship the most important one for Asia-Europe cooperation."
Under the agreements on space research, Japan's space agency NASDA and its French counterpart CNES will work together to develop satellite communications systems.

The accord also envisages joint ventures between French and Japanese satellite companies, such as the Toshiba-Loral consortium which in 1995 won a French Transport Ministry contract to develop a geostationary weather satellite.
At present, over 70 percent of Japanese satellites are launched by the French-led Arianespace firm and the agreement appears aimed at consolidating France's share of Japan's satellite market.
The two countries' space agencies will also work together on future international space stations and multi-space agency voyages to the moon and to Mars.

This may involve cooperation on Japan's launch in 1998 of a Mars probe, called "Planet B", which will be similar to the ill-fated Russian probe which splashed into the South Pacific on Monday, two days after its launch.

The Russian spacecraft carried almost two dozen instruments that had been intended to probe the red planet's secrets. They had been specially created by an international consortium including France, Finland, Germany, Hungary and the United States.
Chirac, accompanied by Telecommunications and Space Minister Francois Fillon and top executives from French aircraft and space firm Aerospatiale, arrived in Tokyo on Sunday for a six-day visit.

The accord reaffirmed French support for Japan to become a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council and agreed the two countries should unite to push through far-reaching reforms in the world body.
